notes.82: Checkmate. Fischer's pieces worked together like an orchestra, while the white queen was left on her own.

parts.title: Understanding each phase
parts.sub: What each phase is for, and its common mistakes

beats.say: Every chess game is a journey in three acts: the opening, the middlegame and the endgame. Each act has its own job.
In the opening, both sides bring out their knights and bishops, fight for the centre and castle to keep the king safe.
Opening mistakes: bringing the queen out early, moving one piece again and again, and forgetting to castle. Here White's queen has moved twice while Black brought out a new piece each time.
The middlegame starts once the armies are out. Now each side needs a plan: attack the king, win a weak pawn or take over an open file. Forks, pins and sacrifices live here.
Middlegame mistakes are moving without a plan, leaving pieces undefended, and attacking with too few pieces. Which plan fits the middlegame?
options: Find a target and bring more pieces towards it
Move the queen out first and check often
Push every pawn as far as it goes
beats.explain: A good plan picks a target and gathers pieces around it.

beats.say: In the endgame only a few pieces are left. The king turns into a fighter and walks to the centre, and every pawn dreams of becoming a queen.
Endgame mistakes: leaving the king at home, pushing pawns before the king can help, and stalemate. Here White is a whole queen up, yet Black has no legal move. That is stalemate, a draw.
Which phase is this?
beats.explain: Only rooks and pawns are left, and the kings can come forward. That is an endgame.

parts.title: Transitions between phases
parts.sub: How and when one phase turns into the next

beats.say: No bell rings at move ten. The opening turns into the middlegame when the pieces are out and the kings are safe. That can happen at move eight or at move twenty.
Clues that the opening is over: the knights and bishops have left home, both kings have castled and the plans begin to clash.
The endgame begins when the queens come off and only a few pieces remain. Trades are the doorway.
Pawns shape the plans. With a locked chain like this, each side attacks where its pawns point: White on the kingside, Black on the queenside.
Some games never reach an endgame. Morphy finished his in the middlegame at move seventeen.
Others travel through all three. Watch the coloured bands under the graph: Fischer's game moved into the endgame once only a few pieces were left.
When does the middlegame begin?
options: When the pieces are out and the real fight starts
As soon as the first piece is captured
beats.explain: There is no fixed move number. Development, trades and pawns decide it.

beats.say: It is only move eight. Which phase is it?
beats.explain: Only kings and pawns are left, so it is an endgame, even at move eight.

parts.title: How strong players win
parts.sub: Small edges, and points versus a winning position

beats.say: Strong players rarely win with one big blow. They collect small edges: a better square for a piece, a weaker pawn, a little more space.
Points are equal here, yet White is better. The knight reaches a dream square, while the bishop is stuck behind its own pawns.
Material counts the pieces: a pawn is one point, a knight or bishop three, a rook five and a queen nine. Useful, but not the whole story. Here White has nine more points, and it is Black to move.
Black is far behind on points. Find the move that wins anyway.
beats.explain: The rook mates on the back row. Points stop mattering once the king is caught.

beats.say: The opposite happens too. Points are equal here, but White is winning: the white pawn queens first, and the white king catches the black one.
Turning an edge into a win takes patience. With an extra pawn, the king leads the way and the pawn follows.
What does the points count leave out?
options: King safety, active pieces and passed pawns
Nothing: the points decide the game
Only how many pawns each side has
beats.explain: A safe king, active pieces and passed pawns can be worth more than points.

parts.title: Traps, sacrifices and comebacks
parts.sub: Why being ahead on points does not guarantee a win

beats.say: A trap is a move that looks like a gift. Watch Legall seem to drop his queen.
Black should have taken the knight instead and stayed only a pawn down. Greed was the real mistake.
A sacrifice gives up material for something bigger: a mating attack, open lines or a pawn that will queen.
In the Immortal Game, Black ended up far ahead on points and still lost. The extra pieces were in the wrong place, and the king had no defenders.
Comebacks happen when the leader relaxes, and a lost-looking position often hides a resource: checks, a stalemate trick or a racing pawn.
You are a rook down and Black threatens mate. Find the move that saves the game.
beats.explain: Check after check: the black king can never escape, so the game is a draw by repetition.

parts.title: Famous historical games
parts.sub: Replay legendary games and guess the masters' moves

beats.say: Now replay four legendary games. Pause any time, try your own idea, and guess what the masters played.
Paul Morphy plays the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard during a night at the opera. Watch how fast development wins.
Anderssen gives away a bishop, both rooks and his queen, and still delivers mate. Count the points as you go.
A thirteen-year-old Bobby Fischer gives up his queen and wins against Donald Byrne. This game passes through all three phases.
One of the most famous endgame puzzles ever. A queen would only draw, so what wins?

parts.title: Visual and interactive learning
parts.sub: Arrows, points, the graph and your own ideas

beats.say: Arrows show the move just played, and glowing squares point at what matters. Here the bishop cuts off the queen and the king at once.
The points bar counts material. The graph shows who the engine thinks is winning, move by move. Here Black is far ahead on points, yet the graph says White is winning.
Your turn to explore. Just before Fischer's famous move, play any move for Black, perhaps saving the queen, and watch the graph answer. Then go back to the real game.

parts.title: Practice and assessment
parts.sub: Name the phase, pick a plan, spot traps and fight back

beats.say: Which phase is this?
beats.explain: The pieces are still coming out and neither king has castled.

beats.say: Move twenty-four, and most pieces are still on the board. Which phase is it?
beats.explain: Everyone is developed and castled, and the queens are still on: the middlegame.

beats.say: The kings have castled on opposite sides. What is a good plan for White?
options: Push the kingside pawns towards the black king
Walk the king back to the centre
beats.explain: With kings on opposite sides, pawn storms open lines without exposing your own king.

beats.say: Only kings and pawns are left. What should each king do?
options: Walk to the centre and help the pawns
Wait while the pawns run alone
beats.explain: In the endgame the king is a strong piece. Bring it forward.

beats.say: The knight on f6 is pinned, so the pawn on d5 looks free. What happens if White takes it with the knight?
options: Black lets the queen go, checks with the bishop and comes out a piece ahead
Black loses the knight on f6
beats.explain: The pin is fake: after the knight takes, the bishop check wins the white queen back with interest.

beats.say: White threatens checkmate on f7. Find a move that stops it.
beats.explain: Guarding f7 or blocking the queen ends the threat, and Black can chase the queen next.

beats.say: You are far behind on points. Find the move that wins anyway.
beats.explain: The queen sacrifice forces the rook to take, then the knight gives a smothered mate.

beats.say: Black has a queen against your rook. Find the move that saves White.
beats.explain: The rook keeps giving check. Your king has no moves, so if Black ever takes the rook, it is stalemate.
